learning.title: now() is the transaction's start, not the statement's
learning.symptom: An integration test asserts rows come back in the order they were written, passes on one run, and fails on the next with the values swapped. Same tree, same migrated database, no code change between the runs. Re-running does not reproduce reliably, so it reads as flake.
learning.cause: PostgreSQL's `now()` is `transaction_timestamp()`: every row written in one transaction gets the same instant, and rows written by two back-to-back transactions can also land on the same instant when both start inside one timer tick. A read ordered by `created_at desc, id desc` then breaks the tie with a UUID, which is to say arbitrarily. The test's expected order came from the order it wrote the rows, and that order is not the order the read promises.
learning.rule: When a test asserts the order of rows written in separate transactions, never derive the expectation from write order if the ordering column is a timestamp. Either read the created values back and sort them the way the query does, or keep the ids from the create responses and apply the query's own documented tie-break. If the test is about ordering, assert the tie-break explicitly; if it is not about ordering, do not assert order at all.
learning.evidence: Bakery #69, `tests/helpers/ticket-admission/operations-integration.ts`. Three `ticket_task_links` rows written by three HTTP calls, then `assertEquals(mine.items[0].linkedTaskIds, [otherTask, taskId])`. Run one: 158 passed / 0 failed. Run two, same tree: 157 passed / 1 failed, `[Diff] Actual / Expected` with the same two ids in the opposite order. `psql -tAc "select pg_get_expr(adbin, adrelid) from pg_attrdef ..."` shows `created_at` defaulting to `now()`.
